    Finally, DHS agrees with commenters' belief that the previous 540-
day automatic extension was too long, as demonstrated by this rule's 
finalization of the IFR's removal of the automatic extension process.
5. Combined Impacts on Individuals, Employers, the Economy, and 
Specific EAD Categories
i. Impacts on Aliens, Families, and Communities
a. General Hardship, Fairness, Educational Disruptions, and Family 
Impacts
    Comment: Many commenters expressed concerns that the IFR would 
cause lapses in valid work authorization, causing job loss or 
interruptions of work, while undermining aliens' financial stability.
    Commenters expressed that lapses in work authorization lead to job 
loss, income loss, housing/food insecurity, loss of health coverage, 
strain on community resources, educational disruption, and harm to 
families and children, and that this is unfair to individuals who have 
complied with all requirements. Many commenters expressed general 
concerns about the consequences of lost wages due to gaps in employment 
authorization. For example, commenters shared that lost wages could 
lead to housing and food



insecurity for nonimmigrants. Several commenters wrote that a lapse in 
employment could make nonimmigrants face the threat of eviction and 
other commenters shared concerns about increased risk of homelessness. 
Commenters remarked that many nonimmigrants may not have families or 
friends to lean on for temporary shelter, making this group 
particularly vulnerable to income shortages. One commenter remarked 
that in the current job market, it would be extremely difficult for 
them to find another job if they were to lose employment due to a lapse 
in work authorization.
    Several commenters expressed concern about the negative impact that 
the IFR would have on families. Some commenters said that employment 
lapses would result in financial insecurity for households. Some 
commenters specifically expressed concern that the IFR would cause 
significant financial hardship for families, including those who depend 
on dual incomes to meet basic needs such as mortgage payments, rent, 
childcare, healthcare, food, transportation, and other living expenses. 
A commenter said that the IFR could force family separation. A 
commenter remarked that a lapse in employment authorization would 
affect nonimmigrants' ability to travel and visit or take care of sick 
family members. Another commenter wrote that work authorization gaps 
would disproportionately affect households where women care for 
children, elders, and disabled family members.
    Several commenters expressed concern regarding the IFR's specific 
impact on children. For example, commenters shared that employment gaps 
would hinder their ability to provide care for their special needs 
children. A commenter remarked that families that continually face 
unmet needs endure stress that can impact the long-term health and 
development of children. Similarly, another commenter wrote that if 
household income is interrupted, children could lose their access to 
stable food, shelter, healthcare, and education ``overnight.'' The 
commenter reasoned that, as a result, children whose parents lack 
stable work authorization are more likely to suffer from poor overall 
health, and have a greater likelihood of hospitalization, school 
absenteeism, and disciplinary issues. Commenters remarked that food 
insecurity from disrupted wages would contribute to conditions such as 
hypertension and diabetes and said that children from poor families are 
four times as likely to be in ``less than very good health'' than 
children from wealthier families. Another commenter similarly remarked 
that they anticipate U.S. citizen children with an immigrant parent to 
be particularly impacted by the IFR.
    A few commenters said that the IFR poses humanitarian difficulties 
and challenges aliens' rights to pursue dignified work, as well as the 
American Dream. Other commenters said that the IFR is inhumane and 
erodes trust in the immigration system, while others stated it sends 
the message that working aliens are dispensable.
    One commenter stated that many EAD applicants are victims of 
disasters abroad and do not need to face further hardship. Similarly, 
multiple commenters stated that aliens come to the United States 
fleeing conflict or persecution and described automatic work 
authorization as ``a lifeline.'' Another commenter described the IFR's 
removal of automatic extensions of EAD validity periods as an unlawful 
form of coercion, stating that it will make life in the United States 
unbearable for aliens. A few commenters expressed concerns about the 
IFR causing potential discrimination in the hiring process. For 
example, a couple of commenters expressed concern that employers would 
not hire employees who are dependent on work authorization, due to 
potential disruptions from processing delays. One commenter remarked 
that the automatic extension policy helps level the hiring playing 
field against potential discrimination.
    A couple of commenters remarked that many nonimmigrant families 
live on modest wages and may not have enough saved up to supplement a 
gap in income. One commenter added that, since asylum seekers are not 
eligible for federal benefits, this group would be left particularly 
vulnerable.
    Some commenters also expressed concerns that nonimmigrants would 
lose benefits such as unemployment insurance and employer sponsored 
health coverage during employment authorization gaps. One commenter 
said that many nonimmigrants rely on EADs to demonstrate their 
eligibility to purchase healthcare on the Healthcare Marketplace. 
Multiple commenters added that, without health care coverage, aliens 
may be more likely to avoid treating health conditions and seeking 
preventive services. Commenters remarked that this would consequently 
increase use of emergency rooms and urgent care and expose nonimmigrant 
populations to medical debt. Additional commenters remarked that the 
2025 tax and budget law, Public Law 119-21, also known as the ``One Big 
Beautiful Bill Act,'' will further limit health coverage for aliens, 
and expressed concern for resulting health outcomes, citing several 
articles which demonstrated correlation between one's ability to afford 
health insurance and their health outcomes. One commenter also remarked 
that some medical insurance plans require minor children to have an 
unexpired EAD for coverage.
    Many commenters expressed concerns about the impact that the IFR 
would have on public resources. Commenters reasoned that loss of income 
would have to be supplemented by increased reliance on public 
assistance programs, charity, and other community or humanitarian 
services. For example, commenters said that the IFR would increase 
demand for services like food pantries, emergency shelters, clothing or 
donation centers, and community health centers. A few commenters 
remarked that these resources are already strained, particularly after 
having absorbed the spillover from shrinking federal assistance 
programs. One commenter remarked that cities in Maine are already 
exceeding their general assistance funds and cannot afford additional 
strain on resources. The commenter added that alien workers fill vital 
roles at social service agencies, working as translators, interpreters, 
case managers, and cultural brokers. The commenter reasoned that loss 
of these workers would exacerbate the strain on these agencies, 
predicting that if the alien workers face a lapse in EAD validity, they 
may then turn to the social service agency for help. The commenter 
added that local support services such as food banks have already seen 
an uptick in demand over the past year.
    Several commenters expressed concern that nonprofit legal providers 
would see an overwhelming increase in demand for services. Similarly, 
some commenters said that crisis-driven requests require timely 
responses and cannot be integrated into existing caseloads without 
sacrificing key legal services, and that shouldering more of these 
cases would cause stress to their organization and divert attention 
away from humanitarian case preparation.
    Response: DHS recognizes that lapses in employment authorization 
can create real hardship for affected aliens, their families, their 
employers and the communities in which they live. Commenters described 
risks such as job loss, reduced income, housing and food insecurity, 
loss of health coverage, strain on community resources, educational 
disruption, and negative impacts on children and family stability, 
particularly for households



relying on dual incomes or modest wages. DHS is also mindful of other 
disruptions that a temporary lapse in employment authorization of an 
alien may bring, including for those who may rely on an automatic 
extension to obtain REAL ID-compliant driver's licenses and other forms 
of identification.
    DHS considered these concerns before issuing the IFR \84\ and again 
in finalizing this rule. However, DHS has concluded that the need to 
ensure proper vetting and screening, and continued eligibility, before 
granting renewed employment authorization and issuing secure evidence 
of that authorization outweighs the risk that some applicants might 
experience a temporary lapse in employment authorization and/or EAD 
validity. DHS also determined that extending this benefit without 
updated adjudication and screening is inconsistent with its mission and 
with E.O.s \85\ directing DHS to ensure that employment authorization 
is not provided to unauthorized aliens and that aliens in the United 
States are vetted and screened to the maximum degree possible.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \84\ See 90 FR 48799, 48809 (Oct. 30, 2025).
    \85\ See E.O. 14159, Protecting the American People Against 
Invasion (Jan. 20, 2025), 90 FR 8443, 8446 (Jan. 29, 2025) and E.O. 
14161, Protecting the United States From Foreign Terrorists and 
Other National Security and Public Safety Threats (Jan. 20, 2025), 
90 FR 8451, 8451 (Jan. 30, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Nevertheless, DHS emphasizes that this rule does not eliminate 
eligibility for employment authorization or prevent eligible aliens 
from obtaining initial or renewal EADs. Rather, it ends the practice of 
automatically extending employment authorization and/or EAD validity 
for up to 540 days based solely on the filing of a renewal application, 
without completion of adjudicative review and related vetting, 
including resolution of any derogatory information. Continued 
employment authorization will now depend on USCIS' approval of a 
renewal application, after USCIS has determined that the alien 
continues to be eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, if applicable.
    This rule also does not change underlying eligibility standards for 
immigration benefits, public benefits, or educational programs, and it 
does not restrict aliens from seeking assistance for which they are 
otherwise eligible under Federal or State law. Certain categories of 
aliens, such as refugees and asylees, remain ``qualified aliens'' for 
specified public benefits under existing statutes, and those 
authorities are unchanged by this rule. Likewise, this rule does not 
alter the ability of States, localities, or private organizations to 
provide charitable or humanitarian assistance.
    DHS also notes that, independent of this rule, it has taken steps 
to reduce the extraordinary EAD filing volumes driven by prior 
policies, including narrowing the use of parole and aligning TPS 
designations with statutory criteria. DHS expects that overall EAD 
filing rates (initial and renewal) will substantially decline because 
of those actions, freeing adjudicative resources to reduce renewal EAD 
application processing times. For example, initial and renewal EAD 
applications for the largest EAD categories that were formerly eligible 
for automatic extensions have significantly reduced since the start of 
2025. See Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
    Accordingly, the decreased EAD filing rates support the point made 
in the IFR that any claims about an increase in the number and duration 
of employment authorization and/or EAD lapses are speculative and 
outweighed by the harm posed by automatic extensions.
    USCIS also publishes current case processing time information on 
its website.\86\ Proper planning by applicants, such as monitoring EAD 
expiration dates, consulting posted processing times, and filing 
renewal applications as soon as permitted by regulation and form 
instructions, can further mitigate the risk and duration of any lapses 
in employment authorization.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \86\ See USCIS, Case Processing Times, https://egov.uscis.gov/processing-times/more-info (last visited Apr. 22, 2026).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Overall, DHS recognizes the seriousness of the hardships described 
by commenters but concludes that, on balance, the national security, 
public safety, and benefit integrity interests served by ending 
automatic EAD extensions outweigh the potential adverse impacts 
associated with temporary lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD 
validity.
b. Mental Health and Vulnerability, Including Risk of Exploitation
    Comment: Commenters asserted that employment gaps due to the lack 
of automatic extensions and processing delays will exacerbate stress, 
trauma, and anxiety, and may push some aliens into unauthorized or 
exploitative employment or unsafe living conditions.
    Multiple commenters remarked that the IFR would instill fear, 
stress, depression, and anxiety, among other mental health concerns. 
One commenter asserted that some of the immigrant population is already 
experiencing significant levels of trauma and stress from immigration 
enforcement activity, and that the IFR would only exacerbate such 
feelings.
    Many commenters shared concerns about nonimmigrants' increased 
level of vulnerability to exploitation by employers and landlords, as 
well as human trafficking, sexual harm, and abuse owing to the IFR's 
elimination of automatic extensions. For example, multiple commenters 
said that loss of employment authorization makes nonimmigrants 
vulnerable to exploitative working conditions. Some commenters remarked 
that if aliens lose their ability to work legally, they may seek under 
the table work or unlawful employment. Commenters warned that this 
leaves such individuals vulnerable to exploitation, explaining that 
these jobs often have lower wages, minimal labor protections, and 
abusive conditions which they may be afraid to report due to unlawful 
status. They also indicated that 84.9 percent of unauthorized 
immigrants reported not being paid time and a half for overtime labor, 
and 37.1 percent reported being victims of minimum wage violations. The 
commenter added that many employers of unauthorized workers do not 
carry workers compensation insurance, meaning that employees may be 
responsible for covering their own medical costs in the case of work-
related injury. The commenter added that since USCIS recently ended a 
program that protected whistleblowers, unauthorized employees are now 
less likely to report various types of abuse. A different commenter 
added that forcing applicants into unlawful employment may also impact 
their eligibility for future immigration benefits, putting them in a 
long-term position of vulnerability.
    Response: DHS recognizes that uncertainty about employment 
authorization and potential lapses in income can contribute to stress, 
anxiety, and other mental health challenges, particularly for 
individuals who may already have experienced trauma or instability. DHS 
also recognizes that economic insecurity and lack of lawful employment 
opportunities can increase vulnerability to exploitation by 
unscrupulous employers, landlords, or others, and may heighten risks of 
trafficking, abuse, or other harm.
    The IFR and this final rule do not deny eligible aliens access to 
employment authorization or to the underlying immigration benefits for 
which they qualify. Rather the IFR, affirmed by this final rule, 
removes only the automatic extension mechanism that previously allowed 
aliens to remain employment authorized for up to 540



days based solely on a pending renewal application, without completion 
of updated vetting and adjudication. As described throughout this 
preamble, DHS has determined that such automatic extensions present an 
unacceptable security and program integrity risk because they confer 
significant benefits before USCIS has completed vetting and screening, 
resolved any derogatory information, determined continued eligibility 
and that the applicant merits a favorable exercise of discretion, if 
applicable.
    DHS cannot structure its regulatory framework on the assumption 
that aliens and/or employers will respond to temporary lapses in 
employment authorization by engaging in unauthorized employment or 
other unlawful conduct. The INA prohibits the knowing employment of 
unauthorized aliens and establishes consequences for both employers and 
aliens who violate those provisions. While DHS recognizes that some 
aliens may face difficult choices if a lapse occurs, DHS does not 
condone unauthorized employment or believe that it is an appropriate 
response to a temporary lapse in employment authorization.
    DHS shares commenters' concerns about exploitation and abuse. DHS, 
including through components such as ICE and USCIS' fraud detection and 
victim protection programs, will continue to enforce laws related to 
human trafficking, forced labor, and other forms of exploitation, and 
to coordinate with the Department of Labor and other agencies on 
enforcement. Existing protections for victims of trafficking, crime, 
and abuse (including T and U nonimmigrant classifications and VAWA) are 
unaffected by this rule. Nothing in this rule diminishes DHS's 
commitment to identify and assist victims or to support the 
investigation and prosecution of traffickers and other offenders.
    DHS recognizes that some aliens may experience heightened stress or 
vulnerability if their employment authorization temporarily lapses. 
However, DHS has concluded that the need to ensure that employment 
authorization is extended only after appropriate vetting and 
adjudication, consistent with current national security and public 
safety priorities, justifies ending automatic extensions. DHS also 
expects that reductions in overall EAD filing volumes may help limit 
the frequency and length of lapses and that timely filing and planning 
by applicants can further reduce uncertainty. For reduced filing 
volumes, see Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
c. Identification, Driver's Licenses, and Access to Services
    Comment: Several commenters expressed concerns that lapses in 
employment authorization and the associated use of employment 
authorization documents would hinder nonimmigrants' abilities to obtain 
or renew their driver's licenses, open and access bank accounts, obtain 
or renew health insurance, enroll in educational programs and training, 
and interact with law enforcement. Commenters remarked that lack of a 
driver's license could interfere with critical daily activities for 
nonimmigrants, such as taking children to school, commuting to work, or 
attending doctors' appointments or immigration hearings. A few 
commenters shared that in many cases, nonimmigrants require driver's 
licenses to perform their job duties and that, without a valid driver's 
license, nonimmigrants may be pushed to drive without a license, 
compromising road safety.
    Response: DHS acknowledges that EADs are commonly used by aliens as 
identity and, in some contexts, status documents for State-issued 
driver's licenses and identification cards, financial services, and 
other purposes. Under the prior automatic extension framework, an EAD 
that was facially expired could be treated as unexpired for certain 
purposes if accompanied by a Form I-797C receipt notice, including 
obtaining a driver's license. As explained in the IFR, DHS determined 
that continuing that practice and the use of automatically extended 
EADs is no longer appropriate.
    This rule does not change State authority to determine which 
documents are acceptable for issuance of driver's licenses or other 
State identification, nor does it amend the Department's REAL ID 
regulations for issuance of driver's licenses or identification cards 
acceptable for federal official purposes defined in the REAL ID Act. It 
does, however, make clear that, for renewal applications filed on or 
after October 30, 2025, a pending Form I-765 and associated receipt 
notice will no longer operate to automatically extend EAD validity 
under DHS regulations. An EAD that is facially expired will not be 
treated as unexpired for employment or immigration purposes unless it 
qualifies for an automatic extension under 8 CFR 274a.13(d) based on a 
renewal application filed before October 30, 2025, or is otherwise 
extended by law or an applicable Federal Register notice (for example, 
certain TPS-related documents).
    The rule does not prevent eligible aliens from seeking or renewing 
EADs, nor does it prohibit States or other entities from accepting 
alternative forms of identification or documentation where permitted by 
law.
    DHS also expects that, as overall EAD filing volumes decline and 
renewal processing times improve, the risk and duration of lapses will 
be reduced. USCIS has already seen a decline in filing rates for the 
main EAD categories that were eligible for automatic extensions. See 
Table 1 in Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
    DHS concludes that the security and benefit integrity gains from 
ensuring that EADs used as evidence of identity and work authorization 
reflect a recent adjudication and completed vetting outweigh the 
potential risks associated with discontinuing automatic extensions.
ii. Employment, Employers, and Economic Impacts
a. Employer Burdens, Business Continuity, and Sector Specific Concerns
    Comment: Multiple commenters argued that loss of automatic 
extensions will increase Form I-9 compliance complexity, cause turnover 
and productivity losses, exacerbate existing shortages in health care, 
education, agriculture, manufacturing, etc., and impose particular 
burdens on small employers.
    Commenters expressed opposition to removing automatic extensions, 
stating that such a change would cause significant disruption to 
employers, including operational inefficiencies (loss of productivity 
and delays), administrative burdens, staffing gaps, human capital costs 
and retention, civil penalties, and compliance burdens as employees 
await renewal decisions without work authorization. A few commenters 
stated that employers could violate Form I-9 compliance rules due to 
unclear authorization statuses.
    Multiple commenters asserted that the IFR would exacerbate existing 
labor shortages and projected a continued decrease in labor force 
participation rates through at least 2030, cautioning that the IFR 
could worsen such shortages by preventing asylum seekers from working 
during EAD processing and removing vetted workers. One commenter stated 
that labor shortages would negatively impact the U.S. economy, hinder 
growth and contribute to inflationary pressures. Another commenter 
stated that a decline of 2 million immigrant workers between 2019 and 
2021 contributed to labor



shortages across sectors, including a labor shortage in the 
construction industry valued at $10.8 billion, reasoning that the IFR 
would replicate such labor shortages across every industry. A commenter 
stated that until public and private sector efforts could fully meet 
industry demand, the United States would need additional workers to 
fill jobs left vacant by the domestic workforce, expressing concern 
that ending the EAD extension could further disrupt workforce stability 
and business continuity for manufacturers. Many commenters stated that 
the removal of automatic extensions would negatively impact critical 
industries and sectors of the U.S. economy that rely on foreign 
workers, including agriculture, technology, energy, manufacturing, 
logistics, transportation, hospitality, education, and construction. 
Several commenters expressed concern about the impact on healthcare and 
healthcare workers, noting that even a brief lapse in employment 
authorization disrupts patient care, clinic operations, and community 
health access. One commenter remarked about how the IFR will adversely 
affect teaching hospitals and academic health systems that employ EAD 
workers.
    Other commenters expressed concerns that the IFR would undermine 
labor unions, collective bargaining, and workforce stability by 
disrupting bargaining units that include immigrant workers with EADs, 
stating that increased risk of sudden job loss among workers would 
strain unions' ability to enforce workplace standards, forcing them to 
devote more resources to protecting vulnerable workers and addressing 
instability caused by the IFR.
    Multiple commenters expressed the importance of automatic 
extensions for business continuity amid persistent government 
processing delays and stated that the IFR would impose unnecessary 
burdens and costs, especially on smaller companies without in-house 
legal departments. Some commenters stated that the rule would force 
employers to conduct extensive contingency planning and workforce 
audits to prepare for potential lapses in work authorization. 
Specifically, a commenter stated that groups such as asylees, who are 
authorized to work incident to status, may still be asked to show an 
EAD to their employer, and further reasoned that the IFR could still 
cause employer confusion and job loss among these groups. Other 
commenters stated that eliminating automatic EAD extensions would cause 
businesses to lose workers and cited to a USCIS analysis establishing 
that EAD extensions previously saved U.S. employers an estimated $3.5 
billion by avoiding labor turnover.
    Numerous commenters expressed concern that employers would be 
forced to terminate employees due to administrative delays in 
processing EAD renewals. Commenters stated that previous sudden 
reversals of work permit rules have created confusion for employers and 
caused them to make rash decisions based on misinformation about 
changing Federal regulations, leading to erroneous layoffs where 
workers with valid EADs were dismissed because employers did not 
understand how to comply with current rules. A commenter said that such 
impacts would exacerbate the ongoing teacher shortage crisis.
    Response: DHS recognizes that some sectors, including healthcare, 
education, manufacturing, agriculture, hospitality, and technology, and 
unionized workplaces may be particularly sensitive to interruptions in 
workforce continuity.
    This rule does not change employers' underlying obligations under 
section 274A of the INA, 8 U.S.C. 1324a, and 8 CFR part 274a to hire 
only individuals who are authorized to work in the United States, to 
verify employment eligibility, and to reverify employment authorization 
when existing documentation expires.
    By ending automatic extensions for renewal applications filed on or 
after October 30, 2025, this rule ensures that employment authorization 
will be evidenced by a secure, unexpired document issued following 
adjudication. This reduces the risk that employers will rely on 
outdated or invalid documentation, and it aligns with DHS's 
responsibility to ensure that employment authorization and/or an EAD is 
provided only after USCIS has completed appropriate vetting and 
determined continued eligibility.
    To ensure that workplaces and businesses have a clear understanding 
of the requirements of the IFR, DHS has updated the Handbook for 
Employers (M-274) and related guidance to assist employers in 
understanding these changes and properly completing Form I-9. Employers 
are responsible for ensuring I-9 compliance for all of their employees, 
including updates to the I-9 verification process.\87\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \87\ See DHS, USCIS, Handbook for Employers M-274, 5.0 Automatic 
Extensions of Employment Authorization and/or Employment 
Authorization Documents (EADs) in Certain Circumstances (last 
updated Oct. 30, 2025), https://www.uscis.gov/i-9-central/form-i-9-
resources/handbook-for-employers-m-274/50-automatic-extensions-of-
employment-authorization-andor-employment-authorization-documents-
eads-in.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS acknowledges that, where renewal adjudications are not 
completed before current EADs expire, some employers may face temporary 
staffing gaps and associated costs. These can include lost 
productivity, overtime for remaining staff, recruitment and training 
for temporary or replacement workers, and internal administrative costs 
associated with planning, auditing, and compliance. DHS discussed these 
categories of impacts in the IFR and in the economic analysis 
accompanying this rule and recognizes there may be negative impacts for 
some employers.\88\ DHS outlined the difficulties in estimating the 
number of EADs that would lapse in the Section V.B.1. of this preamble. 
However, in this final rule DHS has made estimates of economic impacts 
and emphasizes that there is likely to be variation in the impacts, due 
to factors such as dynamic process times, filing volumes, and filing 
behavior. For this reason, DHS provides a wide range for the estimates.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \88\ See 90 FR 48799, 48817 (Oct. 30, 2025). See also Section V 
of this preamble.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS has determined that these operational burdens are outweighed by 
the national security, public safety, and benefit integrity concerns 
associated with automatic EAD extensions. Automatic EAD extensions 
allow employment authorization and/or EAD validity to continue for up 
to 540 days based solely on a pending renewal application, before USCIS 
has completed updated background checks and adjudication. Considering 
current security priorities and E.O.s directing enhanced vetting of 
aliens already present in the United States, DHS has concluded that 
continued reliance on automatic extensions is not an acceptable means 
of managing adjudication backlogs.
    Independent of this rule, DHS has taken steps expected to reduce 
initial and renewal EAD filing volumes by narrowing the use of parole 
and aligning TPS and related policies with statutory text. As discussed 
previously in response to comments, DHS anticipates that overall EAD 
filings will decline and that adjudicative capacity can increasingly be 
focused on timely renewal adjudications.
    DHS notes that an applicant may request that USCIS expedite the 
adjudication of an application that is under USCIS jurisdiction.\89\ 
USCIS considers all expedite requests on a case-by-case basis and 
generally requires documentation to support such



requests.\90\ The decision to expedite is within the sole discretion of 
USCIS.\91\ Expediting a case generally means that USCIS would 
adjudicate a benefit ahead of others, including those who may have 
filed earlier, so USCIS carefully weighs the urgency and merit of each 
expedite request.\92\
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \89\ See USCIS, Expedite Requests, https://www.uscis.gov/forms/filing-guidance/expedite-requests (last updated Sep. 8, 2026).
    \90\ See id.
    \91\ See id.
    \92\ See id.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS recognizes the concerns raised by employers, unions, and 
industry groups and will continue to monitor implementation and 
processing times. Nonetheless, DHS concludes that ensuring that renewed 
employment authorization is granted only after complete vetting and 
adjudication is necessary to better protect national security and 
public safety and to enhance the integrity of the employment 
verification system. Adhering to a system that prioritizes national 
security, public safety, and benefit integrity outweighs the potential 
risks and additional burdens that applicants and their employers may 
face by a potential temporary lapse in employment authorization.
b. Immigrant Contributions to the Economy and Macroeconomic and Local 
Economic Impacts of the Rule
    Comment: Numerous commenters stated that the IFR ignores the vital 
economic contributions of immigrants, and operational realities that 
the work authorization is a critical tool to successfully integrate 
aliens into the United States and contribute to the economy. Commenters 
also stated that the IFR is disrupting businesses that employ these 
aliens and thereby losing the economic contribution of immigrants. For 
example, commenters discussed the positive impacts that asylees and 
refugees make to the U.S. economy and stated that this population 
contributed more revenue than they cost in expenditures to the U.S. 
government. Another commenter said that in 2023, New York State's 
immigrant population represented about 23 percent of the total 
population and paid $74.8 billion in taxes, thus demonstrating that 
immigrants are productive members of the workforce. The commenter also 
stated that a lapse in employment authorization could mean that they 
would lose their homes, face hunger, contribute less taxes to state and 
the federal government or would otherwise become vulnerable (such as 
incurring negative health effects). Another commenter said that 
immigrant workers are a key driver of New York City's economy, making 
up 36 percent of the population; accounting for 37 percent of total 
wage, salary, and business income; and in 2021, contributed tens to 
hundreds of billions of dollars in taxes and spending to the city and 
state. An additional commenter identified in-migration of workers, 
including asylum seekers and other immigrants, as one of the few 
positive trends offsetting the rapid exit of older workers and 
emphasized that many economic development strategies depend on 
immigrants' continuous access to work authorization. Other commenters 
highlighted potential impacts on the economy, pointing out that asylum 
seekers and refugees work in sectors that face shortages and pay 
billions in taxes, and that immigrants will add $7 trillion to the 
economy over the next decade.
    Commenters raised concerns about the macroeconomic impacts of 
eliminating automatic extensions of EADs, such as undermining U.S. 
economic competitiveness, innovation capacity, and national interests 
by forcing workers into temporary unemployment. Other commenters 
predicted that the IFR would lead to negative economic impacts, 
including reduced tax revenue, costs to taxpayers, supply chain 
disruptions, reduced consumer spending, the risk of a recession, and 
job losses. Some commenters expressed general concern that the IFR will 
reduce economic productivity and destabilize the workforce and the 
economy, considering that one in five U.S. workers is an immigrant who 
relies on EADs.
    Commenters said that the IFR would significantly increase States' 
healthcare costs by driving up the uninsured rate among immigrants, who 
already face limited access to Medicaid and Affordable Care Act 
coverage. The commenters remarked that with lapses in work 
authorization eliminating employer-sponsored insurance, States could 
bear nearly $280 billion in uncompensated care costs. The commenters 
also stated that the IFR would adversely impact the States' ability to 
enforce their laws, reasoning that legal workers with lapses in work 
authorization would increasingly enter the underground economy and 
become less likely to report labor and civil rights violations and 
discussed how this would interfere with the States' ability to enforce 
their labor and civil rights laws, because effective enforcement relies 
on employees' ability and willingness to report violations.
    A commenter said the IFR would have significant negative 
consequences on the federal budget and federal agencies such as the 
Internal Revenue Service (IRS) and Department of Labor (DOL) because 
the IFR would reduce the amount of taxable income reported to the IRS 
when applicants face prolonged lapses in employment authorization, 
diminishing federal revenue and complicating federal fiscal 
projections. The commenter further asserted that cutting off work 
authorization for aliens awaiting renewal would push thousands of 
workers into unauthorized employment or out of the workforce entirely 
and consequently increase DOL's investigatory burdens.
    Furthermore, commenters highlighted a range of potential negative 
impacts on the local and state economy, such as disrupting the 
workforce and hindering an alien's ability to maintain consistent 
employment, which, in turn, could directly affect essential community 
services, including infrastructure projects, healthcare, and public 
safety. A commenter highlighted that immigrants play a major role in 
entrepreneurship. Another commenter remarked that Maine stands to lose 
an economic boom they are currently experiencing if immigrant workers 
lose work authorization.
    While expressing concerns about the impacts the IFR's regulatory 
changes would have on the economy, multiple commenters requested a 
return to previous practices allowing automatic extension of EAD 
validity periods.
    Response: DHS agrees that immigrants, including aliens who were 
eligible for the automatic extension of their employment authorization 
and/or EAD for up to 540 days, make important contributions to the 
national and local economies through their labor, entrepreneurship, tax 
payments, and consumer spending; and that continuity of lawful 
employment can benefit workers, employers, and communities. DHS also 
acknowledges the many cited studies, data points, and experiences to 
support their claims about these contributions.
    As the commenters noted, prior DHS rulemakings, including the 2022 
and 2024 temporary final rules and the 2024 final rule, emphasized the 
economic and operational benefits of automatic extensions as a tool to 
mitigate the effects of EAD processing delays. Those rules estimated 
that automatic extensions could reduce wage losses for affected 
workers, avoid turnover costs for employers, and maintain tax 
contributions that might otherwise be impacted by lapses in employment 
authorization. In adopting those measures, DHS gave significant weight 
to the economic and labor market



advantages of continuity of employment.
    The IFR and this final rule in contrast reflect a reassessment of 
that policy and how to balance those economic considerations against 
DHS's core responsibilities for national security, public safety, and 
benefit integrity. DHS has determined that continued use of automatic 
extensions, which allow employment authorization and the related use of 
secure documentation to continue for up to 540 days based solely on the 
filing of a renewal application, before USCIS has completed updated 
vetting, resolved any derogatory information, and determined that the 
alien remains eligible and continues to merit a favorable exercise of 
discretion, if applicable, is not consistent with DHS's current policy 
priorities reflected in, among others, E.O. 14159 \93\ and 14161.\94\ 
Those E.O.s direct DHS to vet and screen aliens already present in the 
United States to the maximum degree possible, to ensure that employment 
authorization is not provided to unauthorized aliens, and to identify 
all resources that may be used to ensure that all aliens who are 
already in the United States, are vetted and screened to the maximum 
degree possible.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \93\ See Executive Order 14159 ``Protecting the American People 
Against Invasion,'' 90 FR 8443 (Jan. 29, 2025)
    \94\ See Executive Order 14161, ``Protecting the United States 
from Terrorist and Other National Security and Public Safety 
Threats,'' 90 FR 8451 (Jan. 31, 2025). See also Presidential 
Proclamation 10949, ``Restricting the Entry of Foreign Nationals To 
Protect the United States From Foreign Terrorists and Other National 
Security and Public Safety Threats,'' 90 FR 24497 (June 10, 2025).
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    Accordingly, ending the practice of providing automatic extension 
of employment authorization documents enhances the benefit integrity in 
adjudications of employment authorization requests and better protects 
public safety and national security by ensuring that aliens are 
properly vetted and determined to continue to be eligible (and merit a 
favorable exercise of discretion, if applicable) for employment 
authorization before such authorization is provided to the alien. DHS 
emphasizes that it is charged with combating unauthorized employment in 
accordance with section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a, which Congress 
implemented, among other reasons, because of the detrimental negative 
effect that unauthorized employment and illegal immigration has on the 
United States and the economy.\95\ In light of these directives, DHS is 
now placing greater weight on security and benefit integrity 
considerations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    \95\ Section 274A of the Act, 8 U.S.C. 1324a was codified as 
part of the Immigration Reform and Control Act of 1986, Public Law 
99-603, for the purpose of controlling illegal immigration to the 
United States by, among other things, establishing penalties for 
employers who knowingly hire undocumented aliens, and prohibit the 
employment of aliens who are unauthorized to work in the United 
States either because they entered the country illegally or are in 
an immigration status which does not permit employment. See H.R. 
REP. 99-682, 46, 1986 U.S.C.C.A.N. 5649, 5649-5650. The legislative 
history reflects that Congress considered, among other things, 
evidence of prior studies demonstrating the adverse impact of 
illegal immigration that warranted legislation to protect U.S. labor 
and the economy. See, e.g., H.R. REP. 99-682, 46-52, 1986 
U.S.C.C.A.N. 5649, 5649-5656.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

    DHS recognizes that ending automatic extensions may result in 
temporary lapses in employment authorization and/or EAD validity for 
some renewal applicants if the adjudication of their renewal EAD 
application is not completed before their current EAD expires. Those 
lapses can lead to lost wages for affected workers, lost output and 
turnover costs for employers, and associated reductions in payroll and 
income tax contributions for the duration of the lapse. DHS also 
acknowledges that such impacts may be more pronounced in certain 
localities, sectors, or communities where EAD holders represent a 
substantial share of the workforce, and that employers and governments 
may face transitional challenges as they adjust to this change.
    While DHS faces uncertainty in projecting the size of any future 
affected population and the magnitude of resulting macroeconomic 
impacts, under several assumptions DHS has estimated the impacted 
population and cost-impacts for a specific window of time. As explained 
in the IFR and earlier in this preamble, EAD processing times have 
fluctuated over recent years due to changes in application volumes, 
programmatic policies, resource levels, and court orders. DHS has also 
undertaken significant policy changes, such as narrowing the use of 
parole and better aligning TPS and related programs with statutory 
criteria, that are expected to materially reduce initial and renewal 
EAD filings over time. Given this evolving environment, DHS estimates 
of the number of renewal applicants who might experience lapses in the 
absence of automatic extensions population, and the resultant impact 
estimates, likely face significant variation. For this reason, we 
clearly articulate the assumptions and inputs relied upon to make the 
estimates and provide ranges for them.
    With respect to commenters' concerns about reduced tax revenues and 
increased uncompensated care, DHS acknowledges that lower earned income 
during periods when some workers are not employed could reduce certain 
tax payments and contributions toward employer-sponsored health 
coverage for those individuals. At the same time, total tax receipts 
and healthcare costs depend on numerous factors across the broader 
economy, and DHS cannot attribute or forecast such aggregate effects 
with sufficient precision to support a quantitative estimate specific 
to this rule.
    DHS also does not agree that ending automatic extensions will 
necessitate or require a shift of large numbers of workers into 
unauthorized employment.\96\ While DHS acknowledges that unauthorized 
work can create an underground labor market where exploitation is more 
likely and enforcement more difficult, this rule does not require or 
condone unauthorized employment. The INA prohibits the knowing 
employment of unauthorized aliens and establishes consequences for both 
employers and aliens who engage in such conduct. See INA sec. 274A, 8 
U.S.C. 1324a; 8 CFR part 274a. DHS will continue to enforce those 
provisions, as well as coordinate with the Department of Labor and 
other agencies on labor-rights enforcement and protection of workers, 
regardless of immigration status. Nothing in this rule alters existing 
worker-protection authorities or the ability of Federal, State, or 
local entities to investigate and remedy labor law violations.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------

that would require future urgent action'').

    DHS further notes that this rule does not change underlying 
eligibility criteria for employment authorization or prevent renewal 
applicants from obtaining employment authorization and/or an EAD. 
Eligible aliens remain able to apply for and receive renewed EADs, and, 
once those renewals are approved, continue contributing economically 
through lawful employment. DHS expects that other policy changes that 
DHS has made will reduce EAD filing volumes, and when combined with 
ongoing process improvements and careful resource allocation within 
USCIS, will lessen the frequency and duration of any future lapses in 
employment authorization and/or EADs.\97\ DHS has seen falling



numbers of I-765 applications since October 2025. See Table 1 in 
Section IV.C.2.i.d. of this preamble.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
